name: Paro Tshechu
image_query: Paro Tshechu mask dance Rinpung Dzong
when: Mar–Apr, five days ending on the 15th day of the 2nd lunar month (lunar calendar)
summary: Bhutan's best-known spring festival: five days of masked cham dances at Rinpung Dzong in Paro, ending before dawn on the last day with the unrolling of a giant thongdrel of Guru Rinpoche. Book rooms months ahead.
body: A tshechu is a festival in honour of Guru Rinpoche, held on or around the tenth day of a lunar month, and every district has one. Paro's is among the largest and the most visited. For five days in March or April, monks and lay dancers in silk costumes and carved masks perform cham dances in the courtyard of Rinpung Dzong and on the ground outside. Each dance has a meaning: some show the defeat of evil spirits, others the judgement of the dead or the eight manifestations of Guru Rinpoche.

The crowd is half the experience. Families from across the Paro valley come in their best gho and kira, sit on the steps and the grass with picnic baskets, and stay all day. Atsaras, masked clowns, move through the audience making jokes and blessing people with wooden phalluses. Children run between the stalls selling sweets and toys. For Bhutanese, watching the dances earns merit, and attending is a social event as much as a religious one.

The final morning is the high point. Before sunrise, a huge thongdrel, an appliqué thangka depicting Guru Rinpoche and his manifestations, is unrolled on the wall of the dzong. Wikipedia notes it is shown only at dawn so that sunlight does not touch it, and it is rolled up again by early morning. Bhutanese believe seeing it frees one from sin. Plan to be there by 4–5 am, dressed warmly, with your guide.
tips: Book Paro hotels three to six months ahead; Tshechu week is the busiest of the year and rates rise.
Dress modestly, with long sleeves; many visitors wear a gho or kira, which Bhutanese appreciate.
Do not walk across the dance ground, block views or use flash; dancers are performing a religious rite.

faqs.q: When is the Paro Tshechu
faqs.a: In March or April, over five days ending on the 15th day of the 2nd month of the Bhutanese lunar calendar. The Western dates change each year, so check the official festival calendar published by Bhutan's Department of Tourism before you book. The thongdrel is shown at dawn on the final day.

faqs.q: Do tourists need tickets for the Paro festival
faqs.a: No ticket is needed to watch the dances, but you must be with your licensed guide and follow the dress code. Hotels and flights cost more in festival week, and the SDF of ₹1,200 per person per night for Indians, or US$100 for others, applies as usual. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the thongdrel at Paro Tshechu
faqs.a: A giant appliqué thangka of Guru Rinpoche and his manifestations, unrolled on the wall of Rinpung Dzong before dawn on the last day of the festival. It is rolled up by early morning so that sunlight does not touch it. Bhutanese believe that seeing it brings liberation from sin.

faqs.q: Can I take photos at Paro Tshechu
faqs.a: Yes, of the dances in the courtyard, from the side and without flash. Do not step onto the dance ground, block other spectators or put a camera in a dancer's face. Ask before photographing people in the crowd. Photography inside temples remains prohibited.

name: Thimphu Tshechu
when: Sep–Oct, three days from the 10th day of the 8th lunar month (lunar calendar)
summary: The capital's great autumn festival: three days of masked dances at Tashichho Dzong's festival ground in September or October, preceded by days of rituals. It falls in Bhutan's clearest season, so it is also the busiest week for visitors.
body: The Thimphu Tshechu is held over three days beginning on the 10th day of the 8th Bhutanese lunar month, which usually falls in September or October. It is preceded by days and nights of prayers and rituals inside Tashichho Dzong, invoking the protective deities. The public dances take place on the festival ground beside the dzong, which allows a much larger crowd than a courtyard, and the capital's population swells with people from the surrounding valleys.

The programme is similar to other tshechus: the Black Hat dance, the dance of the stags and hounds, the dance of the lords of the cremation grounds, and the judgement of the dead, among others. Each tells a story drawn from Buddhist teaching or from the life of Guru Rinpoche. Atsaras, the masked jesters, keep the crowd laughing and carry out a serious job as well, as they are said to protect the dances from harm.

Because it falls in the clear post-monsoon season, Thimphu's festival week is popular with foreign and Indian visitors alike, and hotels fill. If you would like a quieter tshechu, ask your guide about smaller village or monastery festivals in the same months. Indians travelling in the Durga Puja holidays should check whether the festival overlaps; when it does, Phuentsholing immigration and Thimphu hotels are at their busiest.
tips: Book Thimphu hotels at least three months ahead; festival week is the busiest of the autumn.
Arrive early with a cushion or folding mat and a water bottle; good seats on the steps fill by mid-morning.
Wear long sleeves and trousers or a long skirt; a gho or kira is welcome but not required for visitors.

faqs.q: When is the Thimphu Tshechu
faqs.a: Over three days starting on the 10th day of the 8th Bhutanese lunar month, usually in September or October. The exact Western dates change every year, so check the Department of Tourism's festival calendar before booking. The public dances follow several days of rituals inside Tashichho Dzong.

faqs.q: Where is the Thimphu Tshechu held
faqs.a: On the festival ground beside Tashichho Dzong in Thimphu, which holds larger crowds than a dzong courtyard. Rituals in the days before take place inside the dzong. Your guide will know where to sit and how to reach the ground through the festival traffic.

faqs.q: Is the Thimphu festival crowded
faqs.a: Yes. It is the capital's biggest event, it falls in the clearest weather of the year and many international and Indian visitors plan around it. Expect full hotels, higher room rates and dense crowds on the main days. Smaller village tshechus in autumn are quieter alternatives.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to attend Thimphu Tshechu
faqs.a: Watching the dances is free, but you must be with a licensed guide and pay the usual SDF: ₹1,200 per person per night for Indians, US$100 for others under the current incentive. Hotels charge peak rates that week. Check current status before you travel.

name: Punakha Drubchen and Tshechu
when: Feb–Mar, around the 1st lunar month (lunar calendar)
summary: A late-winter festival at Punakha Dzong that re-enacts the 17th-century defeat of a Tibetan army, with local militia in traditional battle dress, followed by the Punakha Tshechu with masked dances and a thongdrel. Warm weather and fewer crowds than Paro.
body: The Punakha Drubchen has its roots in the wars of the Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, who unified Bhutan in the 17th century. Tibetan armies invaded several times, and in one campaign they came to take back a sacred relic, the Rangjung Kharsapani, which the Zhabdrung had brought from Tibet. Bhutanese tradition tells how the Zhabdrung tricked the invaders into believing he had thrown the relic into the river, and they withdrew. The festival commemorates that victory.

Its most striking part is the pazap, men from Punakha's villages who dress as the militia of the time, in traditional battle costume with swords and shields, and re-enact the battle with shouts and war dances in the dzong. There is also a dramatic recreation of the throwing of the relic into the Mo Chhu. Masked dances and rituals continue over several days. The Punakha Tshechu, a newer festival, follows directly afterwards, with cham dances and the display of a thongdrel.

Punakha is warm in February and March, around 15–22 °C by day, and the jacarandas around the dzong may be starting to flower. Crowds are smaller than at Paro or Thimphu, though local attendance is huge. Combine the festival with Phobjikha in the last weeks of crane season, or with Paro and Thimphu. Book Punakha hotels early, as the valley has fewer rooms than Paro.
tips: Check the official calendar; the Drubchen and Tshechu dates move with the lunar year and can fall in February or March.
Stand well back during the pazap re-enactment; the militia move fast and the crowd surges.
Combine with Phobjikha for the last of the black-necked cranes, which leave in mid-February.

faqs.q: What is the Punakha Drubchen
faqs.a: A festival at Punakha Dzong that commemorates the Zhabdrung's 17th-century victory over an invading Tibetan army. Its highlight is the pazap, local men dressed as the militia of the time who re-enact the battle in traditional costume. It is followed by the Punakha Tshechu, with masked dances and a thongdrel.

faqs.q: When is the Punakha festival held
faqs.a: Usually in February or March, around the first month of the Bhutanese lunar calendar. The Drubchen comes first and the Punakha Tshechu follows. Western dates change every year, so check the Department of Tourism's festival calendar before booking, and reserve Punakha hotels early.

faqs.q: Is the Punakha festival less crowded than Paro
faqs.a: With visitors, generally yes, though Bhutanese attendance is large. Punakha has fewer hotels than Paro, so rooms still sell out. The warmer weather in February and March makes it a pleasant festival to attend, and the pazap re-enactment is unique to Punakha.

faqs.q: What is the story of the relic at the Punakha Drubchen
faqs.a: Bhutanese tradition says a Tibetan army came to recover a sacred relic, the Rangjung Kharsapani, that the Zhabdrung had brought from Tibet. He is said to have pretended to throw it into the Mo Chhu, and the invaders left. The festival recreates this scene. It is told as tradition.

name: Jambay Lhakhang Drup
image_query: Jambay Lhakhang Drup Mewang fire blessing
when: Oct–Nov, several days in the 9th–10th lunar month (lunar calendar)
summary: Bumthang's biggest festival, at one of Bhutan's oldest temples. Famous for the Mewang fire blessing, in which crowds run under a burning gate, and for a sacred midnight dance. Held in clear autumn weather in October or November.
body: Jambay Lhakhang, about 2 km from Jakar in Bumthang, is by tradition one of the 108 temples built by the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo in the 7th century. Its drup, a festival of prayers and dances lasting several days, is held in October or November and is the most important event of the year in the Chhoekhor valley. People come from across Bumthang and further east, many camping or staying with relatives, and the temple grounds fill with stalls and families.

The best-known moment is the Mewang, a fire blessing held after dark. A gate of dry grass and wood is set alight, and people run beneath the burning arch to be cleansed of sins and protected from misfortune in the year ahead. Infertile women traditionally pass through it in the hope of conceiving. The heat and the crowd make it intense; visitors watch from a safe distance unless the guide advises otherwise.

Late at night the festival also includes the tercham, a sacred dance performed by masked men without clothes, which is believed to bring blessings and fertility. It is a religious rite, not a spectacle: photography is strictly forbidden, and many guides advise visitors to leave before it unless they are sure they can watch in the spirit intended. The daytime programme includes cham dances in the courtyard, as at other tshechus.
tips: Book Jakar hotels months ahead; Bumthang has few rooms and the festival fills them.
Keep a safe distance at the Mewang fire blessing; sparks fly and the crowd pushes forward.
Do not photograph the midnight tercham under any circumstances; it is a sacred rite and cameras are forbidden.

faqs.q: When is the Jambay Lhakhang Drup
faqs.a: In October or November, over several days in the 9th–10th Bhutanese lunar month. Exact Western dates change every year, so check the Department of Tourism's festival calendar. Plan at least 9–10 nights in Bhutan to reach Bumthang comfortably, or check the domestic flight schedule to Bathpalathang.

faqs.q: What is the Mewang fire ceremony
faqs.a: A fire blessing held after dark during the Jambay Lhakhang Drup. A gate of dry grass and wood is lit, and people run under the burning arch to be cleansed of sins and protected from bad luck. Visitors can watch from a distance; the heat and the crowd make it intense, so follow your guide's advice.

faqs.q: Can tourists watch the naked dance at Jambay Lhakhang
faqs.a: The midnight tercham is a sacred dance believed to bring blessings and fertility. Visitors are sometimes present, but photography is strictly forbidden and the rite must be treated with respect. Many guides advise leaving before it begins. Ask your guide on the day and follow the organisers' instructions.

faqs.q: Where do I stay for the Jambay Lhakhang festival
faqs.a: In Jakar, about 2 km from the temple, in certified hotels or registered farmhouses in the Chhoekhor valley. Rooms are limited and fill months in advance for the festival. Expect ₹3,500–6,000 per room night for a certified 3-star hotel, indicative 2026, with higher rates in festival week.

name: Black-necked Crane Festival
when: On or around 11 November every year (fixed Western date)
summary: A one-day festival in the courtyard of Gangtey Goenpa that welcomes the black-necked cranes back to Phobjikha each winter, with school children's crane dances, folk songs and masked dances. Started in 1998 to support conservation.
body: The Royal Society for Protection of Nature, Bhutan's oldest conservation NGO, started the Black-necked Crane Festival in 1998 with the people of Phobjikha. It is held each year on or around 11 November, the birthday of the Fourth King, in the courtyard of Gangtey Goenpa. The purpose is to celebrate the return of the cranes from Tibet, to raise awareness of their protection among villagers and visitors, and to bring some income to the valley.

The programme mixes culture and conservation. Children from the local school dance in crane costumes, mimicking the birds' movements, and perform songs and short plays about protecting the cranes and their marsh. Villagers present folk dances and masked dances. Stalls sell local crafts and food. Officials and visitors come from Thimphu, and some years the festival marks a special occasion with a larger programme.

It is a small, friendly event compared with the big tshechus, and the best festival for families and wildlife lovers. You can watch the cranes at dawn and dusk on the same day. November in Phobjikha is cold, with nights below freezing, and the valley's few hotels and farmhouses fill quickly, so book early. Your guide and the route permit are needed as for any trip beyond Thimphu and Paro.
tips: Book Phobjikha rooms two to three months ahead; the valley has few beds and the festival fills them.
Watch the cranes at dawn, attend the festival in the late morning, and return to the marsh at dusk.
Pack for frost: nights in Phobjikha in November can fall below 0 °C.

faqs.q: When is the Black-necked Crane Festival in Bhutan
faqs.a: On or around 11 November each year, in the courtyard of Gangtey Goenpa in Phobjikha. The date is tied to the Fourth King's birthday rather than the lunar calendar, so it is easier to plan than most festivals. Some sources give 12 November; confirm the year's date with the Royal Society for Protection of Nature or your operator.

faqs.q: Who organises the Black-necked Crane Festival
faqs.a: The Royal Society for Protection of Nature (RSPN), with the Phobjikha community. The RSPN started the festival in 1998 to celebrate the cranes and raise awareness of their conservation. It also runs the Black-necked Crane Information Centre in the valley.

faqs.q: Will I see cranes during the festival
faqs.a: Very likely. By 11 November most of the cranes have arrived in Phobjikha, and you can watch them feeding in the marsh at dawn and dusk. Keep at least 100 m away and use binoculars. The festival itself takes place in the monastery courtyard, not in the crane area.

faqs.q: Is the crane festival good for children
faqs.a: Yes. It is short, colourful and built around children's crane dances and songs, and the chance to see the real cranes the same day makes it memorable. Dress them warmly for the cold courtyard. It is far less crowded than the big tshechus in Paro and Thimphu.

name: Haa Summer Festival
summary: A two-day festival of Haa valley's herding culture in July, with yak displays, local games, songs and dances, and food such as hoentoe buckwheat dumplings. Started in the early 2010s to bring visitors to Haa in the quiet monsoon season.
body: The Haa Summer Festival was introduced by Bhutan's tourism authority in the early 2010s to draw visitors to the Haa valley in July, a month when few tourists come to Bhutan because of the monsoon. It celebrates the life of Haa's herders and farmers rather than a religious event, so the programme is different from a tshechu: yak and horse displays, local sports, folk songs and dances, and stalls of food and crafts.

Food is a large part of it. The dish to try is hoentoe, buckwheat dumplings stuffed with turnip leaves, cheese and spices, which Haa families traditionally make for special occasions and the new year. You may also find local ara, the home-distilled spirit, dried yak cheese and fresh summer vegetables. Alpine flowers are out on the high meadows around Chele La at this time of year, and the valley is green.

The festival does not run on the same date every year and in some years may not run at all, so check with your operator before you plan around it. July is monsoon season: the road from Paro over Chele La can have cloud, rain and small landslides, and the views are rarely clear. The reward is a quiet, green valley, low prices and a festival where you may be among only a handful of visitors.
tips: Confirm the dates and whether the festival is running before booking; it is not on a fixed date.
Carry rain gear and expect cloud on Chele La; allow extra time for the drive from Paro.
Try hoentoe, Haa's buckwheat dumplings, at the food stalls.

faqs.q: When is the Haa Summer Festival
faqs.a: In July, usually over two days, though the exact dates vary and the event has not run every year. Check with the Department of Tourism or your tour operator before planning. Haa needs a route permit and a licensed guide, as with other districts beyond Thimphu and Paro.

faqs.q: What happens at the Haa Summer Festival
faqs.a: It celebrates Haa's herding and farming culture with yak and horse displays, traditional games, folk songs and dances, and stalls of local food and crafts. It is a cultural festival rather than a religious tshechu. Hoentoe, Haa's buckwheat dumplings, are the food to try.

faqs.q: Is it worth visiting Bhutan in July for the Haa festival
faqs.a: If you like quiet trips and do not mind rain, yes. July is monsoon season, so expect cloud and occasional landslides, but the valley is green, alpine flowers are out and hotels are cheaper. If clear mountain views are your priority, travel in October or November instead.

faqs.q: How do I get to Haa for the summer festival
faqs.a: By car from Paro over Chele La, about 65–70 km and 2.5–3 hours, longer in the rain. Haa is also reachable from Thimphu via Chhuzom. A route permit and licensed guide are required; your operator arranges both. Check current status before you travel.
